newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aristocrat to meet prospectus forecast.
newsitem.headline: Aristocrat to meet prospectus forecast.

text.p: Gaming machine manufacturer Aristocrat Leisure Ltd said on Wednesday the company still expected to meet its prospectus forecast for a pre-tax profit of A$32.8 million for the year to June 30.
Aristocrat Executive Chairman John Dougall told a Securities Institute briefing the company had said in April it still expected to meet its forecasts and "as at today I see no reason to change that."

Dougall said the market had been disappointed with the company's half year result, which had seen a net profit of A$8.3 million and had been looking for a 50-50 split over the two halves to meet its forecast.
"That was not how we had done the budget," he said.
Dougall said Aristocrat was very pleased with its performance since the opening up of New South Wales hotels to club-style poker machines on April 1.
"It is probably going as well as we expected it would," he said.
However, he said the Queensland government had yet to make a decision on privatisation of the gaming industry and uncertaintly had slowed demand.
The developments in both states have been cited by the company as the key factors in their prospectus forecasts.

Dougall said while the company's United States operations would not make a profit for the year to June 30, he expected it would break even pretty quickly and would achieve a profit ahead of a successful licencing application in Nevada.
Aristocrat would not back off from its intention to apply for the Nevada licence before December 1997, he said.

Dougall said Aristocrat, the world's second largest gaming machine manufacturer, saw no reason why it could not make a licensing application for Nevada before December 1997, but any approval would take two to three years to process.

He said it saw opportunities for future growth in interactive television and in-room hotel gaming -- where alliances with other industry sectors, including telecommunications and computer software operators, would be the key -- as well as in in-flight gaming with some international airlines.

Gaming on the internet was a real challenge, with a warning from the Nevada Gaming Commission that such activity would preclude an operator access to its jurisdication, and Aristocrat was "treading pretty carefully", he said.

Subject to government approval in New South Wales, the company was close to being able to offer multi-player gaming, including a horse-racing game which allowed 26 people to play at once, aiming at "the higher rollers", he said.
Dougall said the company was pushing to maintain its strength within Australia, where it had more than 55 percent share of gaming and slot machines.
But it ultimately needed to drive exports, which now accounted for 20 percent of revenue and saw good opportunities in South Africa, Latin America and the Carribean, and Asia, he said.
